sweep_summary: Both sweep items are about Gujarati word stress and both contradict the catalog's Doctor-2004-based 'weight-hedged' (/a/-attracting) coding. Bowers 2019 (open, CC BY, on file since 09-16, re-read: abstract p.1, sections 2, 6, 7 pp.2, 24-25) finds modest acoustic evidence for weakly cued fixed initial stress, no clear acoustic correlate of sonority-driven stress, and inconsistent speaker intuitions. Shih 2018 Phonology 35 remains paywalled (Cambridge 'Get access'; Semantic Scholar CLOSED; CORE no full text; OpenAlex quota exhausted; lingbuzz/ROA searches empty), abstract only: stress 'consistently penultimate, and not sonority-driven', schwa-avoidance left open. Its content is however fully available in two open forms already/now on file: the Rutgers dissertation ch.4 (pp.136-139, 197: 'stress always falls on the penultimate syllable... there is no evidence for sonority-driven stress in Gujarati') and, newly fetched sources this sweep, Shih 2016 'Sonority-driven stress does not exist' (AMP 2015 supplemental proceedings, doi 10.3765/amp.v3i0.3666, pp.1, 8: 'stress always falls on the penult'); the 09-16 pass's 403 was due to a wrong OJS article id (3989 = McCollum), corrected to 3666/3377. Shih & de Lacy 2019 (open, on file) tabulates 13 mutually contradictory descriptions incl. Doctor 2004 and codes Gujarati 'Uncertain'. Best new statement: Bowers 2019 p.25; it supersedes Doctor 2004 as deciding source and supports recoding the record from weight-hedged to positional (initial = penult-of-disyllable) stress with a contested caution. Nothing of high acquisition priority remains; the paywalled Shih 2018 journal text is medium priority for citability only. discovery used DOI resolution, LSA OJS, Cambridge Core, CORE and Semantic Scholar APIs, web.archive.org (no shadow libraries). record: and.

new_statements.quote: The experiments reported here found modest acoustic evidence in favor of fixed initial stress, failed to find clear acoustic correlates of sonority-driven stress as described by de Lacy (2002; 2006), and found that speakers have inconsistent stress intuitions. These results are in keeping with other recent literature on Gujarati (Shih 2016; 2018). On balance, the evidence favors the initial stress analysis of Gujarati. [...] However, it may be premature to discard sonority-driven analyses of Gujarati stress entirely.
new_statements.citation: Bowers, Dustin (2019). Positional vs. sonority-driven stress in Gujarati: New experimental evidence. Phonological Data and Analysis 1(1): 1-28. doi:10.3765/pda.v1art1.19
new_statements.reading: Peer-reviewed instrumental study (acoustics plus speaker judgements) concluding that Gujarati has phonetically weak, fixed word-initial stress with no reliable sensitivity to vowel quality; independently replicated by Shih 2016/2018 (consistent penultimate stress in disyllables, where penult = initial; open dissertation ch.4 p.136-197 and AMP 2016 p.1, p.8 on file). Both instrumental studies name Doctor 2004 among the impressionistic descriptions they fail to confirm. The catalog's 'weight-hedged' coding with /a/ as the strongest weight class encodes exactly the [a]-attraction claim these studies reject; only open-schwa avoidance remains untested. Recode toward positional (initial/penult) stress with a 'conflict'/contested caution citing Bowers 2019, Shih 2018 (and the Turner/Master/Pandit fixed-stress line) against Doctor 2004/Cardona 1965.

audit.recode_to: Positional, phonetically weak stress (initial / penult-of-disyllable; quantity- and quality-insensitive) with an explicit 'contested' caution: impressionistic grammars (Cardona 1965, Doctor 2004, de Lacy 2002) describe /a/-attracting, open-/ə/-repelling stress, but the only two instrumental studies (Shih 2018; Bowers 2019) find no acoustic correlate of vowel-quality-driven stress and support fixed positional stress; schwa avoidance remains untested/open. If the catalog has a 'contested/uncertain' kind, use it; otherwise fixed-initial with caution, not weight-hedged/full-vs-reduced-vowel.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote verified verbatim on Doctor 2004 book p.15 (held page image; djvu text lines 1595-1675 with scanned ə->a noise). (2) The deciding source is a 2004 LINCOM reference grammar that itself calls its stress section 'a minimal overview' of a 'little explored' topic; Glottolog's list (Cardona 1965, Cardona & Suthar 2003, Mistry 1997, Modi 1983/2013) offers only further impressionistic descriptions, which Shih & de Lacy 2019 (fetched sources, pp.20-22, Table 1) show contradict one another on nearly every dimension, Doctor 2004 included. sources.note: Instrumental study (3 experiments: acoustics of initial vs non-initial syllables, acoustics of de Lacy's sonority-driven contrasts, speaker intuitions). Finds weakly cued fixed word-initial stress (initial-aligned F0 low, longer and less coarticulated initial nuclei, more vowel contrasts initially); no usable acoustic correlate of /a/-attraction; speakers 'appear to not have strong intuitions on the relative prominence of syllables within a word' (p.24). sources.quote: Abstract: 'A production experiment was performed to determine the accuracy of the claim that [a] attracts stress away from the default position. Of the five types of phonetic evidence examined, only F1 provides clear evidence for stress, revealing stress to be consistently penultimate, and not sonority-driven. ... However, this paper does not exclude the possibility that stress may avoid schwa (or central vowels).'
sources.note: Peer-reviewed journal version of the instrumental study (the citable form); content duplicated in the held dissertation ch.4, so only the abstract was needed to confirm the finding.

sources.citation: Shih, Shu-hao (2016). Sonority-driven stress does not exist. In G. O. Hansson, A. Farris-Trimble, K. McMullin & D. Pulleyblank (eds.), Supplemental Proceedings of the 2015 Annual Meeting on Phonology. Washington, DC: LSA. 10 pp.
sources.quote: This paper provides new evidence against previous descriptions that stress assignment in Gujarati is sonority-driven (cf. Cardona 1965, Adenwala 1968, Mistry 1997, de Lacy 2002, Cardona & Suthar 2003, Doctor 2004, Schiering & van der Hulst 2010, Modi 2013). I will show that stress in Gujarati is not sensitive to vowel sonority, based on acoustic evidence. Specifically, I will argue that the highly sonorous vowel [a] does not attract stress from the default position – stress always falls on the penult. (p.1) [...] The experimental results from vowel quality and intensity favor the Penultimate hypothesis, rather than the Sonority-Driven hypothesis. (p.8)
sources.locator: section 1 Introduction p.1; section 2.1 p.2 (survey of descriptions); section 4 Results pp.6-8; section 5 Conclusion p.8
sources.note: Early open version of the Phonology 35 experiment: F1 of [a] groups by position (penult vs ultima), not by predicted stress; stress is consistently penultimate in disyllables, [a] does not attract it. Section 2.1 (p.2) notes almost all descriptions agree the default is the penult/initial syllable in disyllables and that they disagree on nearly everything else. Doctor 2004 is named explicitly among the descriptions argued against.
